# Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture proved for every k ≥ 3

The key vector bound (Theorem 2) was found by ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro (Bucić, He, Lee)

Importance: historic (5 of 5)

Researched and written by AI agents (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code). Human editor: Adam Bicz.

The takeaway

A 1970s Erdős–Szemerédi conjecture is claimed proved for every k: families of subsets of [n] with no k-sunflower have size at most c_k^n with c_k < 2. Before this only k = 3 was known, through the 2016 cap-set breakthrough. The authors say ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro found the proof of the central theorem. The paper also says a Lean check exists, but it has not been released yet.

## Key facts

  * Paper: ‘Proof of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower conjecture’, Matija Bucić, Fankang He (Faculty of Mathematics, University of Vienna), Hyunwoo Lee (KAIST and IBS ECOPRO), arXiv 2610.26686 [math.CO], submitted 19 Oct 2026
  * Conjecture (abstract): ‘In the 1970s, Erdős and Szemerédi conjectured that for any n ≥ k − 1 ≥ 2, any collection of subsets of [n] not containing a k-sunflower has size at most c_k^n for some c_k < 2.’ The paper traces the question back to 1970
  * Theorem 1: any subset of 2^[n] with no sunflower of k sets has size at most 2^((1 − 1/(16k³))n). Lower bound (Deuber, Erdős, Gunderson, Kostochka, Meyer): k-sunflower-free families of size 2^(n − O(n log log k / log k)), so the result is ‘not far from best possible for large k’
  * Earlier: Erdős–Szemerédi 2^(n − Ω(√n)); Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang (2019) and Rao give 2^(n − Ω(n/log n)). k = 3 followed from the 2016 cap-set bounds (Croot–Lev–Pach; Ellenberg–Gijswijt) through Alon–Shpilka–Umans; Naslund and Sawin gave base 3/2^(2/3) ≈ 1.89 using Tao’s slice rank
  * Method: Theorem 2 bounds the number V_k(D, n) of vectors in [D]^n without a k-sunflower by the polynomial method (dimension counting with low-degree factors and a Chernoff bound); a reduction (Section 4) transfers the vector bound to set families with D = 16k²
  * AI statement, verbatim: ‘The proof of Theorem 2 was found by ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro, following a short discussion, which started by asking it to generalize the k = 3 case argument in [45], which we needed for our original target of proving the induced variant of the Erdős–Sauer problem. The original argument it produced used the slice-rank terminology due to Tao (as used in [45]); we rewrote it in the polynomial method language … The authors have verified all the results in the paper and take full responsibility for the content. The proof has been verified in Lean 4.35; the verification will be made available on the Palomar repository.’ ([45] is Naslund–Sawin)
  * Concurrent work cited in the paper: another team proves that the set-sunflower relation on the Boolean cube has maximal slice rank, and ‘They discuss extensive use of AI, including multi-agent setups’. The authors say that obstruction concerns set sunflowers, while their tester is for vector sunflowers, so it does not apply
  * Consequences listed in the paper: the vector bound extends the Alon–Shpilka–Umans question (connected to fast matrix multiplication) and gives results in arithmetic property testing and on equal subset sums

## What happened

A sunflower is a family of sets whose pairwise intersections are all the same set. Erdős and Szemerédi asked how large a family of subsets of an n-element set can be without containing k sets forming a sunflower, and conjectured an exponential saving over the trivial 2^n. The k = 3 case became a corollary of the 2016 cap-set breakthrough. Bucić, He and Lee had asked ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro to generalize Naslund and Sawin’s k = 3 slice-rank argument for a different problem, the induced Erdős–Sauer problem. The model produced a bound for vector sunflowers that works for all k, and with the authors’ reduction this gives the full conjecture.

The authors rewrote the model’s slice-rank argument in polynomial-method language. They say all results were verified, including in Lean 4.35, but the formal proof had not been posted when the preprint appeared.

## Why it matters

This is one of the best-known problems in extremal set theory. It sits next to the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture, which stays open, and is tied to cap sets and the group-theoretic approach to matrix multiplication. The authors credit the model with the proof of the key theorem, not with exposition, which puts it among the strongest AI contributions to combinatorics so far. Until the Lean files are released or experts review it, the claim stays pending.

# THE SUNFLOWER CONJECTURE FALLS

Take the numbers from 1 to n and look at all the ways of picking some of them: there are 2ⁿ such subsets. Now pick a few subsets that share exactly the same common part, and nothing else. Mathematicians call this a sunflower: the shared part is the core, and what remains of each set is a petal that touches no other petal.

Sunflowers are a basic tool of combinatorics. The paper lists links to the limits of certain logic circuits, to the “cap set” problem, to fast matrix multiplication and to information theory.

## A question from 1970

The most natural question about them goes back, according to the authors, to a 1970 paper by Paul Erdős. How large can a collection of subsets of {1, …, n} be if no k of its sets form a sunflower?

In the 1970s, Erdős and Endre Szemerédi conjectured that such a collection must be exponentially smaller than the 2ⁿ possible subsets: at most cⁿ, for some number c strictly below 2.

For decades, the best bounds only shaved off a little, never enough to bring the base below 2. Only the three-petal case (k = 3) was settled, in 2016, through the breakthrough on the cap set problem and a reduction due to Alon, Shpilka and Umans.

## The bound

Matija Bucić and Fankang He (University of Vienna) and Hyunwoo Lee (KAIST and the Institute for Basic Science, South Korea) prove the conjecture for every k ≥ 3. Their main theorem: a collection with no k-petal sunflower has at most

3 · (2 − 1/(16k³))ⁿ

members. The base sits just below 2, but it is a fixed number below 2, and that is exactly what Erdős and Szemerédi asked for. A construction from 1997 shows that, for large k, the truth cannot be much lower.

## From sets to vectors

The proof goes through a version of the problem with vectors. Split the numbers into n blocks of D elements and choose one element per block: each choice is a vector. Several vectors form a sunflower when, in every position, their entries are either all equal or all different.

The authors then build a “sunflower tester”: a function that, on a sunflower-free collection, is non-zero only when all its inputs are the same vector. The new ingredient is to write this function, step by step, with interpolation polynomials of low degree. Counting those polynomials bounds the size of the collection (their Theorem 2). A probabilistic argument, random blocks averaged over all set sizes, carries the bound back to ordinary sets.

## Found by a machine, checked by another

The paper’s statement on AI is unusually direct. The proof of Theorem 2 was found by ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro, after a short discussion that began by asking it to generalise the known three-petal argument. The authors needed that step for another goal: an induced version of a graph problem posed by Szemerédi, which they announce for a later note.

The model wrote its proof in the language of “slice rank”. The authors rewrote it in the language of the polynomial method, which they find easier for readers. They state that they verified every result and take full responsibility, and that the proof has been verified in Lean 4.35, a proof-checking software, with the verification to be posted on the Palomar repository.

## What it does not settle

The authors did not try to optimise the base. For three petals, it does not beat the 2017 bound of Naslund and Sawin, about 1.89. And the stronger sister problem, the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture, remains open: their bounds still depend heavily on the block size D, which is exactly what that problem forbids.

L39: ###### Abstract
L40: 
L41: Naslund and Sawin used the slice-rank method for diagonal tensors to prove that
L42: 
L43:  | $$|\mathcal{F}|=O\!\left(n^{1/2}\left(\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}\right)^{n}\right)$$  |
L44: 
L45: for any sunflower-free family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$. We prove a lemma similar to the slice-rank lemma for the newly-defined $i$-triangular tensors, and use it to achieve a polynomial-factor improvement of the bound of Naslund and Sawin by proving that
L46:  | $$|\mathcal{F}|=O\!\left(n^{1/6}\left(\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}\right)^{n}\right)$$  |

L49: ## 1 Introduction
L50: 
L51: Let $[n]:=\{1,2,\cdots,n\}$. For $k\geq 3$, a collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $[n]$ is said to contain a $k$-sunflower if there are $k$ pairwise distinct sets in $\mathcal{F}$ such that the intersection of any pair of them is the same. A family $\mathcal{F}$ is said to be $k$-sunflower free if it does not contain a $k$-sunflower. The notion of a sunflower in set-systems was introduced by Erdős and Rado in [【17†1】], where the following conjecture was made.
L52: ###### Conjecture 1.1 (Erdős-Rado Sunflower Conjecture).
L53: 
L54: For $k\geq 3$, let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $k$-sunflower free family of $m$-subsets of $[n]$, i.e., each set is of size $m$. Then
L55: 
L56:  | $$|\mathcal{F}|\leq\mu^{m}$$  |
L57: 
L58: for a constant $\mu$ depending only on $k$.
L59: 
L60: Later, Erdős and Szemerédi [【18†2】] made the following non-uniform version of the above conjecture.
L61: ###### Conjecture 1.2 (Erdős-Szemerédi Sunflower Conjecture).
L62: 
L63: For $k\geq 3$, let $\mathcal{F}$ be a $k$-sunflower free family of subsets of $[n]$. Then
L64: 
L65:  | $$|\mathcal{F}|\leq\lambda^{n}$$  |
L66: 
L67: for a constant $\lambda<2$ depending only on $k$.
L68: 
L69: In [【19†3】], Naslund and Sawin used the slice-rank method for diagonal tensors to settle the above conjecture by proving that:
L70: ###### Theorem 1.3.
L71: 
L72: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a sunflower-free family of subsets of $[n]$. Then
L73: 
L74:  | $$|\mathcal{F}|\leq 3n\sum_{k\leq n/3}\binom{n}{k}=O\!\left(n^{1/2}\left(\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}\right)^{n}\right).$$  |
L75: 
L76: The slice-rank method for diagonal tensors which is based on the slice-rank lemma of Tao for diagonal tensors [【20†4】] is a polynomial method rooted in a breakthrough paper by Lev, Croot and Pach [【21†5】] and subsequent paper of Ellenberg and Gijswijt [【22†6】].
L77: The slice-rank lemma for diagonal tensors has been generalized to other types of tensors, see for example [【23†7】, 【24†8】]. In [【24†8】], we introduced the notion of higher-order $i$-triangular tensors and proved an analogue of Tao’s slice-rank lemma for such tensors of even order.
L78: In this paper, first we extend the corresponding result to $i$-triangular tensors of any order, then, we apply it to prove our main result given below which is a polynomial improvement on the Naslund-Sawin bound of Theorem 【25†1.3】.
L79: ###### Theorem 1.4.
L80: 
L81: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a sunflower-free family of subsets of $[n]$. Then
L82: 
L83:  | $$|\mathcal{F}|\leq O\!\left(n^{1/6}\left(\frac{3}{2^{2/3}}\right)^{n}\right).$$  |
L84: This paper is organized as follows. In Section 【7†2】, we briefly explain the slice-rank method and then the slice-rank lemma for $i$-triangular tensors is proved. Section 【8†3】 contains a brief account of the Naslund-Sawin theorem. In Section 【9†4】, our 1-triangular tensor for sunflower-free families of sets is presented, and in Section 【10†5】 the bound of Theorem 【26†1.4】 is derived.
L85: ## 2 $i$-Triangular slice-rank lemma
L86: 
L87: Let $A_{i}$, $i=1,\ldots,k$, be some finite sets and $\mathbb{F}$ be a field. A $k$-tensor $T$ is a function from $\prod_{i}A_{i}$ to $\mathbb{F}$. A tensor $T$ is called a slice if it can be decomposed as $T=fg$ where $f$ is a 1-tensor from $A_{j}$ to $\mathbb{F}$ for some $j$ in $[k]$ and $g$ is a $(k-1)$-tensor from $\prod_{i\neq j}A_{i}$ to $\mathbb{F}$. The important notion of the slice-rank of a $k$-tensor is as follows.
L88: ###### Definition 2.1 (Slice-rank).
L89: 
L90: Let $T\colon\prod A_{i}\longrightarrow\mathbb{F}$ be a $k$-tensor. The slice-rank denoted $\operatorname{sr}(T)$ of $T$ is the minimum $r$ such that $T$ can be written as the sum of $r$ slices, i.e., $\operatorname{sr}(T)$ is the minimum number $r$ such that
L91: 
L92:  | $$T=\sum_{i=1}^{r}f_{i}g_{i}$$  |
L93: 
L94: where for every $i$, $f_{i}$ is a 1-tensor from $A_{j}$ to $\mathbb{F}$ for some $j$ in $[k]$ and $g_{i}$ is a $(k-1)$-tensor from $\prod_{i\neq j}A_{i}$ to $\mathbb{F}$ .
L95: When $A_{1}=\cdots=A_{k}$, a $k$-tensor $T$ is diagonal if $T(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})\neq 0$ implies that $a_{1}=\cdots=a_{k}$.
L96: 
L97: The following lemma has been at the heart of the slice-rank method with diagonal tensors.
L98: ###### Lemma 2.2 (T. Tao [【27†9】]).
L99: 
L100: Let $A$ be a finite set and $\mathbb{F}$ be a field. If $T\colon A^{k}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}$ is a diagonal $k$-tensor with non-zero diagonal entries, then $\operatorname{sr}(T)=|A|$.
L101: As the notions of slice-rank and usual rank coincide for matrices, i.e. 2-tensors, the above lemma can be considered as the natural generalization of the fact that square-matrices with non-zero diagonal entries are full rank. Thus, naturally, one wonders whether it is possible to generalize the other facts about the ranks of special matrices to higher-order tensors.
L102: What follows in this section can be viewed of a generalization of the fact that triangular matrices with non-zero diagonal entries have full rank. As it was mentioned earlier, in [【24†8】], we introduced the notion of higher-order $i$-triangular tensors and proved a lemma similar to the slice-rank lemma of Tao for even-order tensors. Here, the corresponding lemma, Lemma 【28†2.5】 in this paper, is proved for tensors of every order. First, we recall the definition of an $i$-triangular tensor.
L103: ###### Definition 2.3.
L104: 
L105: Let $(A,\leq)$ be a totally ordered finite set, and $\mathbb{F}$ be a field. A $k$-tensor $T:A^{k}\to\mathbb{F}$ is $i$-triangular if $T(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})=0$ whenever $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})$ is off-diagonal and $x_{i}\leq x_{j}$ for all $j\neq i$.
